content_blocks.title: With Great Power Comes Great OPSEC
content_blocks.content: Mimikatz is the Swiss Army knife of credential extraction — and the most monitored tool on earth. Every EDR vendor has signatures for it. Running `mimikatz.exe` on a live system is like walking into a bank robbery wearing a nametag. Learn the technique, understand the detection, and always use the quietest method available. Your engagement depends on it.

content_blocks.title: Mimikatz and LSASS Credential Extraction
content_blocks.content: **Mimikatz** extracts credentials from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process, which caches authentication material including NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and (on older configurations) plaintext passwords. The **sekurlsa** module is the primary credential extraction engine: `sekurlsa::logonpasswords` dumps all cached credentials, `sekurlsa::wdigest` targets WDigest plaintext, `sekurlsa::kerberos` extracts Kerberos tickets. Mimikatz requires SeDebugPrivilege (typically Administrator) to access LSASS memory. Modern Windows mitigations include Credential Guard (virtualization-based), LSA Protection (RunAsPPL), and Windows Defender Credential Protection.

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: LSASS and Mimikatz
content_blocks.content: Windows has a security guard called LSASS who holds all the keys to the building. LSASS keeps copies of passwords, ID cards, and master keys so people don't have to re-authenticate every time. Mimikatz is like picking the guard's pocket — it reaches into LSASS's memory and pulls out all those keys. That's why Microsoft added locks (Credential Guard) to make the pocket harder to pick.

content_blocks.title: Mimikatz Credential Extraction Commands
content_blocks.content:
```
mimikatz # privilege::debug          # Enable SeDebugPrivilege
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords   # Dump all cached credentials
mimikatz # sekurlsa::wdigest          # WDigest plaintext passwords
mimikatz # sekurlsa::kerberos         # Kerberos tickets
mimikatz # sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp  # Load offline dump
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords   # Dump from offline dump

# Kerberos ticket operations
mimikatz # kerberos::list              # List cached tickets
mimikatz # kerberos::ptt <ticket.kirbi>  # Pass the ticket

# OPSEC-improved alternatives:
# 1. Dump LSASS with comsvcs.dll (no Mimikatz binary on disk)
rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll MiniDump <lsass_pid> C:\lsass.dmp full
# 2. Use SharpKatz or Rubeus for .NET in-memory execution
# 3. Use LSASS Shtinkering for cross-version compatibility
```

content_blocks.title: Real-World: OPSEC-Aware Credential Harvesting
content_blocks.content: During a red team engagement, running `mimikatz.exe` on a target triggers Defender within seconds. Instead, the operator: (1) dumps LSASS using `comsvcs.dll` (a legitimate Windows DLL), (2) exfiltrates the minidump, (3) runs Mimikatz offline against the dump on the operator machine. Detection on-target: only a minidump write event (EID 10 in Microsoft-Windows-Diagnosis-Scripted/Operational). The credentials are the same, but the EDR footprint is minimal. Lesson: the technique matters more than the tool.

content_blocks.title: Mimikatz Modules: SKKP
content_blocks.content:
**SKKP** — the four Mimikatz modules you'll use most:
- **S**ekurlsa — Credential extraction (logonpasswords, wdigest, minidump)
- **K**erberos — Ticket operations (list, ptt, golden, silver)
- **K**ommunikat — SMB/DC communication (DCSync)
- **P**rivilege — Token manipulation (debug, elevate)

Remember: **S**ekurlsa gets the goods, **K**erberos uses the tickets, **K**ommunikat talks to DCs, **P**rivilege opens the door.

content_blocks.title: Detection and Defense Scenario
content_blocks.content:
You're a blue teamer who discovers these events on a workstation:
- EID 4656: Process accessing LSASS with SeDebugPrivilege
- EID 4688: rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll MiniDump
- LSASS memory spike followed by file creation in C:\Temp\

1. What technique was used?
2. Why wasn't `mimikatz.exe` detected directly?
3. What defensive controls would prevent or detect this?
4. How would you harden LSASS on future systems?

Think from both sides of the engagement.

content_blocks.title: Know the Defense to Beat the Defense
content_blocks.content: The best red teamers understand blue team detection as deeply as they understand exploitation. If you run Mimikatz without considering Sysmon EID 10, Defender signatures, and EDR behavioral detection, you'll get caught. Understanding detection makes you a better operator AND a better defender. Study both sides. The credential is the prize; the OPSEC is the game.
